analysis:
Examined the add-on busy signaling changes: new ProviderBusy.swift (reason enum, since_ms, addon bundle id), the register path in ProtocolCodec.swift (lines 226-230), and the App Attest worker resume guard in ProviderLoop+AppAttestShadow.swift (lines 115, 120). The Messages.swift head excerpt covers only CoordinatorMessage, which is unchanged. The provider-side Register/Heartbeat Codable edits are visible only as patch ranges and are not in the supplied text.

The busy fields are provider-to-coordinator advisory metadata (TB-002). They carry a closed reason enum, an int64 timestamp and an optional bundle id string. They contain no secrets or prompt data and are not authorization inputs. A malicious provider could omit or forge them, but the coordinator remains authoritative: routing eligibility is gated by attestation and App Attest checks, and busy only signals draining, so a forged claim does not widen serving permission. Busy is emitted beside status draining, which stops routing even if the coordinator ignores the unknown fields.

The raw-attestation register encoder mirrors the new fields, which matches the file comment requiring every Register field to be mirrored. Decoding an unknown reason as absent is fail-safe.

The guard change from servingDrain.refusing to refusingForServiceChange in resumeAppAttestWorkerAfterUpdate means an add-on hold no longer blocks resuming the App Attest worker after an update. That is plausibly intended: the worker stays available so challenge handling is not delayed (see the 2026-10-10 availability note). The definition of refusingForServiceChange is not in the supplied evidence. If it fails to cover an update-driven or shutdown drain, the worker could resume during a service change. This is not provable from the supplied evidence.

No new finding is supported. A reviewer should verify the servingDrain semantics (refusing vs refusingForServiceChange) and the Messages.swift Register/Heartbeat encode and decode edits, which are not in the supplied text.
